translations.text: The saying of Hippolytus: an interpretation concerning David and Goliath.
1.1. The counsels of the blessed David, who lived under the Old Law, who was a prophet in song and perfect in deeds, are easy to know for those who know the holy books with faith. 1.2.
Who would not marvel at this blessed David, who from his youth inscribed the counsels of Christ on his heart?
1.3. Or who would not marvel at the words that were spoken and made manifest by him?
He who was [?] by God rightly as king and as a chosen prophet, who informed us not only about the things in which we now are and those that are past, but also about those that are yet to come.
2.1. Now which of his qualities shall I praise first: the valor of his deeds or the prophecies of his words?
For in both we find this prophet, in word and in deed, made like his Lord. 2.2.
I find him a shepherd of sheep; I understand him to have been secretly anointed king; I see the tyrant struck down by him, and I know of the combat brought to an end,
and I see the people freed from slavery; and after this I see him hated by Saul, fleeing from him as an enemy and a schemer, and hunted,
hidden in the wilderness; and he who had earlier been hated by Saul was established as king over Israel.
3.1. Now who would not call blessed those righteous patriarchs, who proclaimed beforehand the things to come not only in word
but also in deed, and who accomplished through suffering what was done to Christ?
And truly it must be understood, this matter that lies before us: what the blessed prophets did beforehand, whether by word or by spiritual deed. 3.2.
These types and deeds are shown with a view to the things that were to come, on account of him who was destined in later times to be the fulfiller of the law and the prophets;
he came into the world to make the truth manifest, he who came and revealed himself to us through the Gospel and said:
"I am the way and the truth and the life", for he was righteous and true and the Savior of all. 3.3.
How should we not understand what was done beforehand by the blessed David, and was afterward accomplished by the Redeemer and given by grace as a gift to the holy churches?
4.1. We must first recount the type concerning the latter things, so that one may be able easily to understand what has been said as well.
These two anointings were performed by the blessed Samuel: one upon Saul and one upon David.
But Saul came forward to that anointing by his own self-will, not as one worthy before God, but as a mere man, a transgressor of the law;
and the man who was asked for as king was brought upon them in anger as a persecutor.
For in the same way Herod, a man who transgressed the law, at one time reigned over sinful men. 4.2.
And David was anointed secretly in Bethlehem, for the heavenly King was destined to be born in Bethlehem; and he, anointed not secretly by the Father, was made manifest in the world,
as the prophet says: "Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions." 4.3.
And Saul was anointed from a horn as if of earthenware, for his kingship was transient and was quickly shattered.
But David was anointed with the horn of power, since it had been announced beforehand through the prophet concerning him who by the precious horn would show forth victory over death.
And David himself, in the psalms, says prophetically: "And may he deliver my lowliness from the horns of the unicorn."
And Moses, prophesying in like manner, says in the blessings:
"The firstborn of the bull, his is the beauty; his horns are like the horn of a unicorn, and with them he shall strike down the nations." 4.4.
For this reason too the Lord commanded Samuel and said to him: "Fill this horn of yours with oil, and I will send you to Bethlehem, for I have found among the sons of Jesse a king for myself."
Through the prophet he shows us beforehand the things that are to come. 4.5. And Saul was reigning over Israel;
and David had been secretly anointed. Because of his disobedience the Holy Spirit departed from Saul, and that evil spirit from the Lord entered into him. 4.6.
This is fitting, for the transgressor of the law must be handed over into the hands of a harsh angel.
And David, the one chosen from the heart of God, was adorned with heavenly wisdom;
for this reason too the book bears witness and says: "And David was understanding in all things, and the Lord was with him."

5.1. He was a young man and tended the flock of Jesse his father, just as Christ was the Son made a child, from the Father, and by becoming a child was shown by the Father to be truly a shepherd to the saints. 5.2.
With good order he arranged the psaltery; and he shows us the seven-stringed harp itself, and by striking its string he sent up blessing to heaven,
and he clearly foretells the counsel to all, and he drives the evil spirit out of Saul. 5.3.
Saul became jealous of him and came to hate him, and watched for a chance to kill him, as though he were someone who had done him evil;
and deceitfully he set him as a commander over the people and appointed him to fight on the people's behalf. He intended somehow to throw him into the hands of the Philistines. 5.4.
He was pleasing in the eyes of the people, for he was the one who went in and came out before them,
and he delivered the people from enslavement to the nations, and with the sword he took vengeance on the godless and unbelieving.
6. When the Philistines saw this, they were stirred up; and when they saw his strength, they were astonished.
And they gathered their camp for battle at Socoh of Judea, and they encamped between Socoh and Azekah, at Capharnaim.
And Saul and all the people of Israel gathered in the valley and made ready for battle against the Philistines;
and the Philistines stood on the mountain on one side, and the Israelites stood on the mountain on the other side; and a single valley lay between them.
And there came forward a man from the race of the Philistines, whose name was Goliath of Gath.
His height was four cubits and a span; and there was a helmet of brass on his head;
and his coat of mail had scales [?] like those of a mail for laying on [?], which he had put on, and the weight of his mail was three thousand shekels of bronze;
and there were bronze greaves on his legs, and a bronze shield on his shoulders, and the shaft of his spear was like a weaver's beam, and the head of his spear was six hundred weights of iron.
And the one who carried his armor went before him. And he stood and called out to the camp of the Israelites and said: "Why do you come to fight against us?
Am I not a Philistine, and you Hebrews of Saul? Choose for yourselves a man who will come out against me;
and if it happens that he overcomes me, we shall be your slaves; but if I overcome him and kill him, you shall be our slaves and serve us."
And that Philistine said to them: "Behold, I reproach you today; now send out a man, and let us meet one another in combat."
And Saul and all Israel heard that word of the Philistine, and they were greatly afraid.
7.1. And because the Philistines were stirred up at the time when they saw David, and raised up war against them,
this foretells to us the one who was to be revealed from David, the Savior of the world; and the unbelieving nations marveled at his name and persecuted the saints. 7.2.
And the two mountains that are shown foretell to us the two laws: the one that was by written letter, and the second that was by grace. 7.3.
But as for what it says, that there was a valley between them: for the place that was between the two mountains is called a valley,
so that by this it might show the enticement; and it likens the desire of this world to that valley, toward which people, through desire and disobedience, perish. 7.4.
And as for what it says: "There came out a mighty man from the camp of the Philistines,
and his name was Goliath," this foretells to us that the devil was doing his own will through the Philistines, equipped as if with armor,
prepared for war against the world, to dishonor the saints and to heap reproach on the circumcised. 7.5.
Therefore he says boastfully: "Am I not one Philistine, and you Hebrews of Saul?"; and he is openly reckoned a foreigner and an unbeliever in God. 7.6.
Therefore the writing and the measure were set forth in the midst, so that through those things by which he grew strong we may understand.
And what it said, "four cubits and a span," showed us the four ends of the earth, over which the devil displayed his tyranny. 7.7.
And as for the span of which it speaks: it is because he grew insolent and began to come out against God;
and therefore he shall be cast out [?] by God himself, shown to be a son of the devil, whose figure Goliath bore beforehand. 7.8.
And as for what it says, that the links [?] of his mail had the thickness of a manacle, this plainly shows us the hole of the serpent and its many cunning devices of biting. 7.9.
And as for its speaking of the five hundred weights of his mail: it is because five thousand years passed, and after five thousand years the Savior of the soul came to battle,
but in the likeness of men he arrayed his own flesh for battle.
And just as Goliath was struck down by David, so too the deceiver was defeated by Christ. He cut off the head of the serpent. 7.10.
"Goliath's helmet of bronze was on his head, and greaves of copper were on his legs."
It shows us his arrogance and his terrifying character, equipped with armor of various kinds.
And that foreign man did not appear to the world in the way he was made in the beginning.
Along with this it also speaks of a sword, for arrogance was in him, in those words of filthy reproach. 7.11.
And where it says, "a shield of bronze on his shoulders," it speaks of the round compass of the whole world being gathered to him and seized by him, as John says:
"The whole world is in tottering [?]." 7.12. And the shaft of his spear was like a weavers' beam;
Of what webs does it speak, if not of those who devise vanity and are subject to the devil?
As Isaiah says: "Their web shall not be of use for clothing, for they weave as a spider's web, for their deeds are deeds of lawlessness." 7.13.
For it says, "The head of his spear was six hundred weights." It shows us that the deceiver, who is the Antichrist, is prepared to come under the name of God.
8.1. This man, puffed up in heart and trusting in his armor, stood between them, cried out with insolence and said:
"Send out a man who will come out to fight me, and let the two of us go out against each other." 8.2.
Do you see, beloved, that this speech is strange and full of the power of the devil?
For when he said, "Let him come out against me," he showed now that the things that happen in this world do not happen through anything else,
but through the one by whom it was done in the beginning through Cain, who killed his brother Abel, and who first spread murder and envy and greed in the world.
And now, through him, by the mouth of Goliath, he reviled David and held all the people in contempt.
9.1. When Saul saw his armor, and that unimaginable terror, and the height of his stature,
and when he heard the great boasting of his words, he was afraid and became terror-stricken in heart;

It was necessary for Saul to tremble with that fear, so that the blessed David might be glorified and that contest might be accomplished through him, and so that the one who attacks us might be put to shame and defeated. 9.2.
And because the devil was a tyrant over all, and easily seized all, and swallowed all alive, for this reason he shouted through the mouth of Goliath and said:
"Send out a man, and let us fight each other"; for no one was found by whom anyone could match his armor.
10.1. Now this one had been shown to be a tyrant over all and had shut them in [?] by the fear of death.
The blessed David said to Saul: "Let not the heart of my lord the king tremble; your servant will go out and meet that foreigner." 10.2.
By this he foretells to us that the attacker will be defeated in every way by the boy David; and Saul was a fearful man,
for he reasoned in human terms and did not understand the power of the Word, because of which he said to him: "You cannot go out against that foreigner;
you are a boy, and he is a fighting man from his youth." 10.3. Do you see that the Scriptures plainly show us the truth?
And when he said, "You are a boy," he showed the power of the Word dwelling in him, who was a young boy,
handsome and fair of form to the eye, for he had from the Father the authority of judgment, slender of body in appearance, great in spiritual understanding.
And Saul held David back with words and made him hesitate, for he said to him, "He is a fighting man from his youth," and by this he shows us what had come to pass.
For from the beginning the deceiver overthrew everyone by warfare, and with his own venom and sting he struck the man in paradise:
Eve, and through her Adam; and then Cain, for he stirred up envy against his brother; and after this those giants:
through lust he sowed in them his own unsound seed; and through Ham he mocked the nakedness of the father.
And then through Esau he drove Jacob away; and then through the patriarchs he had Joseph sold into Egypt; and through Pharaoh he brought curses and evils upon the people;
against whom he made war a second time, in the wilderness as well, and when they were sated and drunk he filled them with idol-worship,
and he sent biting serpents upon them, and sowed lust in them through fornication with the daughters of the Midianites;
and he separated them all from God and struck them down in the wilderness; and then he armed Goliath and put him forward as a champion, with such words as were heard by Saul.
11.1. Blessed David heard, and he was not afraid and did not tremble, but said:
"Your servant was tending his father's sheep, and it would happen that whenever a lion or a bear came and snatched something from the flock, I would pursue it and take it out of its mouth;
and I your servant killed both the lion and the bear; and if it rose up against me, I would turn on it and seize it by the throat and strangle it on the spot.
Now let this foreigner be counted as one of them. Shall I not go out and overthrow him and wipe away the reproach in Israel today?
Or who is this uncircumcised foreigner, who taunts the camp of the living God?
And the Lord who delivered me from the mouth of the lion and from the arms of the bear, he will deliver me from the hands of this uncircumcised foreigner."
And Saul said to him: "Go out, and may the Lord be with you." 11.2. O blessed voice, with the divine word that was spoken by the mouth of blessed David!
Tell me, O blessed David, how could a lion and a bear become a help to a shepherd of sheep, or when did you take a living sheep out of their midst?
11.3. Certain writings are able to bear witness for you about this;
if anything of the kind did happen with you, still you are prophesying about things that were prepared; I know that you are prophesying and not lying. 11.4.
For the true David has come, who was born from your womb, beforehand, of a virgin, and who shepherded his Father's flocks,
and he killed death as the lion, and wiped out the sin of this world as the bear, and drove away that deceiving wolf, and raised up man as a dead sheep,
and with the wood he crushed the head of this serpent, and rescued Adam from the lower depths of hell, like a dead sheep, from death. 11.5.
These are the words you spoke beforehand to Saul, so that we too might learn of the righteous shepherd, and through him glorify the Father made known by him.
12.1. Now that you have come, blessed David, teach us those spiritual counsels: how you do battle with Goliath without armor.
Saul arms you with earthly armor, but you cannot fight with it, for you are unaccustomed to it;
therefore cast aside human knowledge and take what has been granted to you from above by God.
The helmet set upon your head, for you have an unfading crown prepared in heaven;
You have put on that coat of mail, which is faith, your body clothed with the love of Christ;
you carry the sword from your heart, for you have the word that came down from heaven dwelling within you;
you also have the shield before you, having acquired the power of the Holy Spirit, by which you are able to quench the arrows of the wicked one;
and because all this is with you, you were not afraid of the tyrant. 12.2. Besides these things, you show us something else:
you have a pouch, as a shepherd does, by which you foreshadow to us the Church, from which you draw milk, as it were, to delight many.
And you put into it five round stones from the brook: you foreshadow to us the five laws in the Church, as rest in the new law.
You also have a staff with you, for by this design you foreshadow to us Christ, the King and High Priest.
You also have in your hands a sling, which is the commandment of the Law: "You shall love the Lord your God." 12.3.
Good is that armor of yours, O blessed David; it is greater than Goliath, stronger than iron and bronze.
How could this earthly thing be equal to that heavenly one? Or what comparison is there between this perishable thing and that imperishable one?
Or what can human knowledge do beyond that which has been given to you by God?
Therefore you appeared unarmed to the eyes of that unbelieving Goliath, but with that heavenly power you were armed on every side, with faith and fear toward God and with an upright mind,
which was made manifest by God alone, whereas the human mind is unable to see it.
13.1. When the Philistine saw this he said: "Am I a dog, that you come against me with a staff and a stone?
Come out to me, and I will give your flesh as food to the birds of the sky." And the Philistine cursed David by his gods. 13.2.
Do you see that Goliath confessed with an open heart, calling himself a dog and unclean?
David was not afraid of him, nor of the word he had spoken, nor of that gleaming armor, nor of that terrifying height; but he said to him:
"You come against me with sword and spear, and I come to you in the name of the Lord Almighty, from this camp of the Israelites, whom you reproach today.
And God will deliver you into my hands, and I will give your flesh and the flesh of your people as food to the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth;
and let all know that there is a God in Israel."
14.1. When the tyrant Goliath heard this, he became enraged with wrath like a beast;
he thundered, trusting in his own strength, and he despised David as a boy and reproached his God.
And he gave no thought to his own death, nor to the judgment of God.
At once he was filled with wrath and rushed at David, trusting in his armor;
with a swift [?] he raised up his body, shook his armor and tossed his head; his heart pounded within him, he bellowed like a bull and roared like a lion.
And he raised his shield up to his own height, and displayed in his right hand the flashing spear, and stood;
not as if he were doing battle against a man, but as if he meant to break through walls of iron;
he grew enraged, and fastened his armor together, and stood in the middle of the camp, and called out against blessed David. 14.2.
And it was a strange new sight: the whole race of the Philistines stood on the mountain on one side;
they watched Goliath in his arrogance, and did not know what was going to happen to him. So too Saul and all his people stood on the mountain on the other side;
they too watched David, and no small fear was upon them, for they saw a young man, unarmed, facing a full-grown man who could not be withstood;
every man on this side and that watched the contest, but they did not know what was going to happen to him.
15.1. And David prayed to God in his heart, while Goliath boasted of his armor; David knew that it is not by sword and spear that the Lord saves his servants.
He drew near, took out a stone and put it in the sling, hurled it, and struck him on the forehead; it broke through the helmet and sank into his brain, and he fell on his face upon the ground. 15.2.
Wonderful, beloved, are the things that were devised here. It would have been fitting for Goliath to fall from that wound, to fall backward from the [?] of the stone;
but because what was to happen was to be spiritual and not human, so that the power of God might be shown in this too, the wounded Goliath fell on his face,
so that he might bow down before the victorious Word of God who was with David, whom no one is able to overcome. 15.3.
Blessed David stood over him, drew out the man's own sword and cut off his head, and displayed his victory,
just as Christ, when he crushed the head of the serpent, displayed his power over him.
And at that moment, when the Philistines saw their mighty man overthrown, they scattered this way and that.
But the sons of Israel, made victorious through David, trampled their camp, as was said by God:
"Behold, I have given you authority to trample on serpents and scorpions and the devil and all his powers." 15.4.
And David, when he had cut off Goliath's head, brought it and set it down among the people and said:
"Gather, all you servants of God, and see a new thing devised: a man slain by his own sword, as the devil is overthrown by his own wickedness." 15.5.
And he lifted his eyes on high and said: "Is this the man who plotted evil against you?
But now he lies fallen and dead. This mouth spoke great words against God, but now it is deprived of voice.
This was the tongue that reproached you, but now it is bound and silenced.
Were these the eyes that intended evil against you? But now they have remained in a dead man."
16.1. At that time, when Jonathan the son of Saul saw David bringing the head of the Philistine in his hand, he loved him in his heart,
and Jonathan stripped off his finery and put it on David, along with his belt and his armor and his sword and his bow and quiver. 16.2.
What took place is trustworthy. It was incumbent on that people, who knew the Law, concerning Christ the King descended from David, who won the contest on their behalf,
to strip all their glory from themselves and give it to him by whom the devil was [?], death was halted, and Israel was set free. 16.3.
And the church flourishes through singing and offers up song together with the glory of God, for that scripture says:
"The dancers came out to meet David, and they said: Saul has struck down thousands, and David tens of thousands." 16.4.
Who were those who came out to meet him, if not the churches, which are set upright by faith, and confess the Lord and King, and offer up the tens of thousands to him?
Or who were those tens of thousands, if not the nations of men who are believers in this world?
Tens of thousands of angels in the heavens glorify the King who was born in the heavens, and tens of thousands of men praise the child who was born from David,
and the souls of all the holy martyrs await the one who will appear from heaven, who will raise them up. 16.5.
But Saul's heart grew angry at this, because they gave him only the thousands, and when he heard it, he was stirred up; and then another Goliath was revealed.
Tell me, O Saul, what evil did the son of Jesse do to you, he who killed your enemy, the one who plotted evil?
Why do you envy the righteous one, if what was done by him was glorified by God, and now, having become incarnate, he is glorified in the heavens with the Father?
You are king over only six thousand, but Christ is king over all creatures.
You are king over the men of the earth, but Christ over those of heaven, of earth, and of the underworld.
You are king as a man of the times of this passing world, but Christ is the eternal King and abides perfect, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
